UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities 
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
v. 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.

MOTION FOR LEAVE AND ANSWER OF 
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) moves for leave and submits this 
answer1 in response to the Indicated Transmission Owners’ fourth answer in this proceeding, and 
the belated claims of their new witness, Danielle S. Powers.2  Nearly every party in this proceeding 
agrees that the PJM Tariff is unclear and confusing and requires clarification.3  The Indicated 
Transmission Owners do not contend otherwise.  Nor do they offer any evidentiary rebuttal to 
Constellation’s expert testimony on (1) the critical national interest in expediting the efficient 
interconnection and co-location of data center loads,4 (2) the lack of any resource adequacy 
 
1 Constellation submits this answer and motion for leave pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules 
of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213, and respectfully submits there is good cause for the 
Commission to accept the motion for leave.  See Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) 
(accepting answers that “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making”); 
Saltville Gas Storage Co., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in 
understanding the issues raised[] and will ensure a complete record”). 
2 See Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (filed June 3, 2025) 
(“Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer”) and Declaration of Danielle S. Powers (“Powers Decl.”), attached thereto; see also 
Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (filed Mar. 24, 2025) (“Indicated TOs First Answer”); Answer of 
the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (filed Apr. 23, 2025) (“Indicated TOs’ Second Answer”); Answer of the 
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to the Motion to Stay Proceedings at 3-4 (filed May 7, 2025) (“Indicated TOs’ 
Third Answer”). 
3 See Motion for Leave and Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (filed May 8, 2025) (“Constellation’s 
Second Answer”), at 2-9 (summarizing the parties’ positions on this core point). 
4 See Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (filed April 23, 2025) (“Constellation’s First Answer”), Exh. 
1, Declaration of Dr. Paul Stockton; see also Exh. 1 hereto, Rebuttal Testimony of Zachary Ming (“Ming Rebuttal”)

2 
concerns caused by co-location versus load growth generally,5 (3) the much higher transmission 
upgrade costs caused by large loads not locating near generation,6 (4) the use of the transmission 
system under co-location configurations from an expert electrical engineering perspective and how 
that use differs from front-of-the-meter configurations,7 and (5) the broad system benefits of the 
co-location of large loads and generation.8   
Instead, several weeks after the deadline for timely filings in this proceeding, based on the 
schedule outlined by the Commission in its Show Cause Order,9 the Indicated Transmission 
Owners recently submitted a pleading full of misstatements of the record and a few new but 
irrelevant arguments.  The only accompanying evidence was the Powers Declaration, which 
purports to respond to the Testimony of Zachary Ming, Constellation’s witness on the rate design 
issues associated with large loads.  Consistent with PJM’s eight co-location configuration options, 
Mr. Ming advocated for three classes of transmission service for large loads:  firm, generator-
contingent, and interruptible, with corresponding transmission rates reflecting actual use of the 
transmission system.10  The objective is to reliably utilize the transmission system most fully at 
lowest overall cost.  Instead of addressing the merits of Constellation’s rate arguments, Ms. Powers 
misstates the record, makes flawed assumptions, and propounds numerous erroneous arguments.  
 
at 13 (citing Energy and Environmental Economics, Inc. report that “even under a ‘moderate’ data center growth 
scenario, electric demand could double in [Virginia] over a 25-year period. Under an ‘unconstrained’ scenario, the 
time to double is reduced to 10 years”). 
5 See, e.g., Constellation’s First Answer, Exh. 3, Affidavit of Aaron Patterson. 
6 Id. 
7 Id., Exh. 4, Affidavit of Steven Herling (“Herling Aff.”). 
8 Id., Exh. 5, Affidavit of Michael Kormos (“Kormos Aff.”). 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”) at P 87 (PJM and the 
Transmission Owners filings were due 30 days after the Show Cause Order, with responses due 30 days thereafter).  
The Commission’s process did not provide for Transmission Owners to file their initial expert testimony 103 days 
after the Show Cause Order.  (The Show Cause Order issued on February 20, 2025; the Indicated Transmission Owners 
filed their initial expert testimony on June 3, 2025—103 days later.) 
10 Constellation’s First Answer, Exh. 2, Testimony of Zachary Ming (“Ming Testimony”).

3 
To ensure an accurate record, Constellation attaches hereto as Exhibit 1 the Rebuttal Testimony of 
Zachary Ming.   
In addition to Mr. Ming’s rebuttal of Ms. Powers’ declaration, Constellation—rather than 
responding to points it previously covered—instead offers the following brief clarifications to the 
record: 
First, the Indicated Transmission Owners claim that “[p]arties have lost sight of something 
throughout the course of this proceeding,” which according to the Indicated Transmission Owners, 
is that “FERC cannot order a new type of service unless there is a finding that the existing 
arrangement is unlawful.”11  But it is the Indicated Transmission Owners who appear to “have lost 
sight” of the detailed explanation in Constellation’s comments—comprising 23 pages, with 
additional supporting expert testimony—that the existing rate is unjust and unreasonable because 
it lacks sufficient clarity about the rules for co-location.12  The Indicated Transmission Owners 
have no answer.  Constellation also submitted a separate answer itemizing the positions of every 
party in this proceeding on this issue, listing the parties supporting the Commission’s preliminary 
finding that the PJM Tariff does not contain “provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or 
consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements” and 
“[t]he absence of such provisions may leave entities unable to determine what steps they can or 
must take to effectuate co-location arrangements of various configurations.”13  Indeed, nearly 
every party in this proceeding agrees that the existing PJM Tariff requires clarification about how 
to serve large loads.14   
 
11 Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 13 (emphasis added). 
12 Constellation’s First Answer at 13-36 (citing statute, cases, and supporting evidence); see also Ming Testimony at 
19-24 (providing expert testimony on the same showing); Ming Rebuttal at 5-6 (repeating showing in initial 
testimony). 
13 Constellation’s Second Answer at 2-3; see Show Cause Order at PP 74-75. 
14 See Constellation’s Second Answer at 2-9.

4 
Second, the Indicated Transmission Owners belatedly trot out the “major questions 
doctrine” to argue that the Commission does “not have any authority to require a new type of 
transmission service” and “cannot order any of the replacement rates contemplated by the 
parties.”15  This smacks of desperation.  In at least six rounds of prior filings in these proceedings, 
the Indicated Transmission Owners never previously raised this argument.16  And it is no wonder 
why: it is meritless.  Confirming that existing behind-the-meter generation rules in PJM apply to 
large loads, and adopting generator-contingent or interruptible forms of transmission service with 
accompanying rates, is well within the Commission’s statutory authority to ensure just and 
reasonable and non-discriminatory rates for transmission service, and is far narrower in its scope 
than, for example, the Commission’s recent transmission reforms in Order No. 1920, let alone 
Order No. 888.17  Ironically, if any party’s position implicates the “major questions doctrine,” it is 
the Indicated Transmission Owners’:  Congress expressly left to the states jurisdiction over retail 
power sales, yet the Indicated Transmission Owners ask the Commission to override a state’s 
choice to allow co-location and direct retail service by mandating that all large loads must be 
wholesale Network Integrated Transmission Service customers and pay on a gross basis.18 
 
15 Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 14 & nn. 42, 43 (citing cases). 
16 See Indicated TOs’ First, Second, and Third Answers (all failing to raise “major questions” issue); see also Exelon 
Comments in Opposition to Complaint, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (filed Dec. 12, 2024); Exelon Answer and Motion 
for Leave to Answer Constellation and Vistra Answers, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (filed Jan. 7, 2025); Comments of 
David Weaver, PE on Behalf of Exelon (Docket No. AD24-11-000) (all also failing to raise “major questions” issue). 
17 See, e.g., Bldg. for the Future Through Elec. Reg’l Transmission Plan. & Cost Allocation, Order No. 1920, 187 
FERC ¶ 61,068 (2024), order on reh’g & clarification, Order No. 1920-A, 189 FERC ¶ 61,126 (2024), order on reh’g 
& clarification, Order No. 1920-B, 191 FERC ¶ 61,026 (2025); Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open 
Access Nondiscriminatory Transmission Services by Public Utilities; Recovery of Stranded Costs by Public Utilities 
and Transmitting Utilities, [Regs. Preambles 1991-1996] FERC STATS. & REGS. ¶ 31,036 (1996), 61 Fed. Reg. 21,540 
(1996), order on reh’g, Order No. 888-A, FERC STATS. & REGS. ¶ 31,048 (1997), order on reh’g, Order No. 888-B, 
81 FERC ¶ 61,248, 62 Fed. Reg. 64,688 (1997), order on reh’g, Order No. 888-C, 82 FERC ¶ 61,046 (1998), aff’d in 
relevant part sub nom., Transmission Access Policy Study Group v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667 (D.C. Cir. 2000), aff’d sub 
nom., New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1 (2002). 
18 See Constellation’s First Answer at 26-28 (explaining that requiring co-located loads to always take Network 
Integrated Transmission Service unduly limits state jurisdiction and flexibility contrary to law) (citing cases).

5 
Third, the Indicated Transmission Owners repeat allegations that “BTMG [Behind-the-
Meter Generation] is not similarly situated to behind-the-meter load” because “co-located load 
arrangements use and rely upon the transmission system and therefore cannot qualify as BTMG.”19  
The Indicated Transmission Owners continue to simply assume the premise of this argument 
without any expert evidentiary support for the claim.  Ms. Powers does not address it.  Instead, the 
Indicated Transmission Owners leave unrebutted the only expert engineering testimony that is in 
the record on this point by Steven R. Herling, a former Vice President of Planning for PJM with 
over 30 years’ experience in the operations and planning of the transmission system.  He explained 
that these two configurations (BTMG and co-located loads and generation) can be designed “in 
exactly the same manner.”20   
In addition, the Indicated Transmission Owners’ new diagram purporting to show that the 
location of the meter has no effect on the amount of grid services used by a configuration in fact 
confirms that there is no meaningful difference between BTMG and co-located loads:  simply 
remove the word “large” throughout the Indicated Transmission Owners’ illustration and the same 
diagram depicts BTMG.21  As Mr. Ming already testified, “[t]here is no physical, technical, or 
 
19 Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 16-17. 
20 Constellation’s First Answer, Exh. 4, Affidavit of Steven R. Herling at ¶ 30 (“BTMG arrangements and co-located 
load arrangements can be designed from an engineering perspective in exactly the same manner.  In one, the load is 
typically greater in magnitude than the generating facility.  In the other, the load is typically lesser in magnitude than 
the generating facility.”); see also id. (“The physics of energy delivery are the same in both arrangements and are not 
related to contractual arrangements or rate structures.”). 
21 Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 7 (illustration of “Large” Load Meter Scenarios, depicting a “Large” Load and a 
“Large” Generator).  Note also that the Indicated Transmission Owners’ diagram also fails to depict protective 
relays—the electrical equipment that does change usage of the transmission grid (meters do not).  See Constellation’s 
First Answer at 46 (showing a generator-contingent (behind-the-meter) configuration with protective relays); see also 
id. 48-49 (relying on expert engineering testimony to refute the Indicated Transmission Owners’ and others’ 
unsupported and erroneous assertions that protective relays cannot be relied upon to prevent power flows).  The 
Indicated Transmission Owners and their sponsored witness both repeat these false claims that protective relays cannot 
work.  See Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 9-10; Powers Decl. at ¶ 14 (“It is not at all clear that the relay schemes 
and protection mechanisms … would protect the grid”).  However, Ms. Powers could have, but did not, challenge the 
testimony of Steven Herling or Michael Kormos, which specifically affirmed the widespread use and efficacy of relay 
schemes and protection mechanisms in PJM operations and designs.  See Herling Aff.at ¶ 23; Kormos Aff. at ¶ 7.

6 
economic reason why a netting construct should apply differently for customers with behind-the-
meter generation or co-located generation.”22      
Fourth, Indicated Transmission Owners claim that any form of transmission service other 
than full Network Integrated Transmission Service “would represent a significant departure from 
NERC Reliability Standards FAC-002-2 and TPL-001-5” and “[t]he result would be reduced 
scrutiny of load” and “mismanagement of the transmission system,” among other reliability 
allegations.23  They are incorrect.  NERC Reliability Standard FAC-002-2 states that “[e]ach 
Transmission Planner … shall study the reliability impact of: (i) interconnecting new … electricity 
end-user Facilities and (ii) materially modifying existing interconnections of generation.”24  No 
one is advocating that co-located load should be connected without a study.  Worse still, unrebutted 
record evidence shows that some Indicated Transmission Owners are refusing to “work on … 
requests to co-locate load with … generators at certain facilities,” which appears to be a plain 
violation of FAC-002-2.25   
Ms. Powers, for her part, cites recent load drops in ERCOT as proof that large loads 
jeopardize reliability.26  But as Mr. Ming testifies, the dropped load in ERCOT was not co-located; 
it was grid-connected.27  The Indicated Transmission Owners previously raised the same type of 
 
22 Ming Testimony at 55. 
23 Indicated TOs’ Fourth Answer at 21. 
24 NERC Reliability Standard FAC-002-2 R1.  NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5 is about Transmission Planners 
maintaining system models for performing planning assessments.  The Indicated Transmission Owners do not explain 
how all other potential types of transmission service necessarily violate this Reliability Standard. 
25 See Show Cause Order at PP 74-75 (the Commission preliminarily finding that the “absence of [clear co-location] 
provisions [in the PJM Tariff] may leave entities unable to determine what steps they can or must take to effectuate 
co-location arrangements of various configurations” and this “raises the potential for undue discrimination or 
preferential treatment”).   
26 Powers Decl. at ¶ 13.   
27 Ming Rebuttal at 17.

7 
reliability concerns about grid-connected large load drops in Virginia.28  It is misleading for the 
Indicated Transmission Owners to keep repeating claims that co-location jeopardizes reliability 
but then citing load drops by grid-connected loads.  For reasons that Constellation already fully 
explained, it also is misleading to claim that co-location jeopardizes resource adequacy when co-
location has no effect on it whatsoever—load is load that must be served, whether it is co-located 
or grid-connected.29 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, Constellation respectfully requests that the Commission grant leave and 
accept this answer and adopt its preliminary finding that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable 
and unduly discriminatory and preferential because it lacks clear provisions for the treatment of 
large loads co-located with generation, and this lack of clarity has caused undue discrimination 
against large loads seeking to co-locate.  The Commission should fix replacement rates as set forth 
in Constellation’s First and Second Answers.  The Commission should not order a stakeholder or 
other process that relies on the good faith and cooperation of the Indicated Transmission Owners 
to resolve the issues raised in this proceeding.   
 
28 See Constellation’s First Answer at 22 (pointing out that Virginia load drops were of grid-connected load, not co-
located load). 
29 See id. at 58-63 (explaining misplaced resource adequacy concerns).
